headline: The Bell phone system is broken up
text: On 1 January the Bell System ceased to exist as one company. AT&T was ordered to separate from its local phone companies, which become seven regional companies. Bell had assets of 150 billion dollars and more than a million employees.

headline: Ray Kroc, the man behind McDonald's, dies at 81
text: Ray Kroc died on 14 January in San Diego. He built McDonald's from a single burger restaurant into 7,500 outlets in the United States and 31 other countries and territories, with systemwide sales above 8 billion dollars in 1983. His own fortune was about 600 million dollars.

headline: Apple unveils the Macintosh at $2,495
text: Apple presented the Macintosh on 24 January, two days after a 1.5 million dollar commercial by the film director Ridley Scott ran during the Super Bowl. The Mac is worked with a mouse and pictures on the screen, has a 9-inch screen and 128 kilobytes of memory, and costs 2,495 dollars.

headline: Supreme Court: Sony may sell video recorders for home use
text: On 17 January the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 for Sony in the Betamax case, which started in 1976 when Hollywood studios sued. The court said the makers of video recorders cannot be blamed when owners copy TV shows, because recording a programme to watch later is fair use.

headline: Nestle signs a deal with the baby-milk boycott groups
text: On 25 January Nestle and the International Nestle Boycott Committee signed a joint statement backing the World Health Organization's code on selling baby-milk substitutes, and named four areas where Nestle will do more. The American group INFACT immediately suspended its boycott of Nestle products in the US, which had run since July 1977.

headline: Boeing's 737-300 makes its first flight
text: The new 737-300 flew for the first time on 24 February. It is the second generation of the 737 jet and has new CFM56 engines, which give better fuel economy and less noise.

headline: Chernenko replaces Andropov in the Kremlin
text: Konstantin Chernenko succeeded Yuri Andropov as Soviet general secretary on 13 February, four days after Andropov died. Chernenko was 72 and in poor health, with emphysema and heart failure, and many saw him as a stopgap leader who gave the Politburo's old guard time to pick a successor from a younger generation.

headline: Michael Jackson wins a record eight Grammys
text: Michael Jackson won a record eight Grammy awards on 28 February, including Album of the Year for Thriller and Record of the Year for "Beat It". On 7 February the Guinness Book of Records named Thriller the best-selling album of all time, with more than 30 million copies sold.

headline: BMW shows the M5, a very fast saloon
text: At the Amsterdam motor show in February BMW showed the M5, a four-door car tuned by its racing division, BMW Motorsport. BMW's reputation is for sporty cars.

headline: Sam Walton keeps his bet and dances the hula on Wall Street
text: On 15 March Wal-Mart's founder Sam Walton put on a grass skirt and danced the hula in Wall Street, as promised. He had bet that his company could not make an 8% pre-tax profit in 1983. It did.

headline: Disney's first Touchstone film, Splash, opens
text: Splash opened on 9 March as the first release under Touchstone Films, a new Disney label for films aimed at more grown-up audiences than the usual Disney cartoons and family movies. The mermaid comedy starred Tom Hanks and Daryl Hannah, and it was made for $11 million.

headline: Berkshire's book value is up 32%, and Buffett has bought a furniture store
text: Berkshire Hathaway's yearly report shows value per share up 32% in 1983, to 975.83 dollars. It bought Nebraska Furniture Mart, merged with Blue Chip Stamps and now counts about 2,900 registered shareholders, up from 1,900.

headline: The prime rate rises to 11.5%
text: Banks raised their prime rate from 11% to 11.5% on 19 March, after holding it at 11% since August 1983. Borrowing is getting dearer again.

headline: British coal miners go on strike
text: The National Union of Mineworkers began a strike on 12 March, after the National Coal Board said on 6 March it would close 20 pits and cut about 20,000 jobs. About 142,000 miners were involved, although more than a fifth of them, especially in Nottinghamshire, kept working from the start.

headline: The prime rate climbs to 12%
text: Banks raised the prime rate to 12% on 5 April, the second rise in under three weeks. It was 10.5% in February last year.

headline: US scientists announce the virus that causes AIDS
text: On 23 April US health secretary Margaret Heckler announced that a virus called HTLV-III is the cause of AIDS. US health officials had first recognised the disease in 1981, so for three years doctors had been treating patients without knowing what caused it.

headline: A police officer is shot outside the Libyan embassy in London
text: Policewoman Yvonne Fletcher, aged 25, was fatally shot on 17 April while policing a demonstration outside the Libyan embassy in London, and shots came from its windows. A siege of the building followed. Britain broke off diplomatic relations on 22 April, and the siege ended on 27 April when the 30 Libyan staff left.

headline: Intel's annual report celebrates its first billion-dollar year
text: Intel's report for 1983 shows sales up 25 percent to more than 1 billion dollars, the first time it has passed that mark. Chairman Gordon Moore wrote: "We closed 1983 with a bang." The recovery has brought strong demand for chips for electronics and personal computers.

headline: A run on Continental Illinois, one of America's biggest banks
text: Large depositors pulled out over 10 billion dollars from Continental Illinois of Chicago in early May. It was the seventh-largest US bank, with about 40 billion dollars in assets, hurt by oil loans it had bought from the failed Penn Square Bank. In mid-May the US authorities put together 7.5 billion dollars of aid for the bank.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_Illinois (read 2026-10-03, citing New York Times of 18 May 1984); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Square_Bank (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Swiss voters keep their bank secrecy
text: On 20 May Swiss voters rejected, by 73% to 27%, a proposal "against the abuse of bank client confidentiality and bank power" that aimed to weaken bank secrecy. Swiss banks such as Bankgesellschaft, Bankverein and Kreditanstalt would have had to change how they treat customers' data.

headline: The Soviet Union will skip the Los Angeles Olympics
text: On 8 May the Soviet Union said it would boycott the summer Olympics in Los Angeles. It comes four years after the United States led a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Games. Relations have been bad since the Soviets shot down a Korean airliner last September.

headline: Apple has sold about 70,000 Macintoshes since January
text: By 3 May Apple had sold about 70,000 Macintosh computers since the launch on 24 January. The Mac cost $2,495 and had only 128 KB of memory, which made it hard for programmers to write software for it, so buyers had fewer programs to choose from than on rival computers.

headline: Disney pays $325 million to a raider to go away
text: In June financier Saul Steinberg offered to buy 37.9% of Disney at 67.50 dollars a share. Disney instead bought back his shares at 70.83 dollars each, a profit for him of about 32 million dollars. With expenses the cost was about 325 million dollars. Paying a raider to leave is called greenmail.

headline: The prime rate reaches 13%
text: Banks raised the prime rate to 13% on 26 June, its fourth rise since March, when it stood at 11.5%. The prime rate is what banks charge their best business customers, so a higher rate makes loans more expensive for companies and for people buying homes.

headline: Virgin Atlantic flies its first passengers
text: The airline Virgin Atlantic made its first flight on 22 June, from London Gatwick to Newark in New Jersey. Its owner Richard Branson used a leased Boeing 747 named Maiden Voyager and sold tickets through Virgin record shops.

headline: A gunman kills 21 at a McDonald's in San Ysidro, California
text: On 18 July a gunman killed 21 people at a McDonald's restaurant in San Ysidro, California. A police sniper killed him 77 minutes into the attack.

headline: Maradona is sold to Napoli for a world record fee
text: Barcelona sold the footballer Diego Maradona to Napoli for 10.48 million dollars on 1 July, a world record. His time at Barcelona had gone badly after a broken ankle and a brawl in the Spanish cup final. On 5 July about 75,000 fans came to watch him being presented at Napoli's stadium, a club that was fighting to avoid relegation.

headline: General Electric buys Employers Reinsurance for 1.075 billion dollars
text: GE paid Texaco 1.075 billion dollars in cash for Employers Reinsurance, one of the three largest US companies that insure insurers against big claims. It has 800 employees. GE put it under a new financial services company, together with GE Credit, which has 16 billion dollars of assets and leases equipment to other firms.

headline: McDonald's Olympic promotion runs short of food
text: McDonald's promised free food for every American medal ("When the U.S. wins, you win"). With the Soviet Union boycotting, the United States won 174 medals and supplies ran short at more than 6,000 restaurants.

headline: IBM launches the PC AT with Intel's 80286 chip
text: IBM introduced the PC AT in August. It uses the Intel 80286, the chip Intel launched in 1982.

headline: Zola Budd and Mary Decker collide in the Olympic 3000 m final
text: On 11 August the American Mary Decker, the favourite, collided with the barefoot runner Zola Budd of Britain in the Olympic 3000 metres final in Los Angeles. Decker fell with a hip injury and was carried off in tears, and Budd finished seventh. She was first disqualified but reinstated an hour later, and Maricica Puica of Romania won.

headline: Nestlé agrees to buy Carnation for $3 billion
text: On 4 September Nestlé of Switzerland agreed to buy the American food company Carnation for 3 billion dollars, or 83 dollars a share, in a friendly takeover. It is the biggest acquisition outside the oil industry so far. Carnation makes evaporated milk, hot cocoa mixes, ice cream novelties and dog food.

headline: Disney names Michael Eisner and Frank Wells to run the company
text: On 22 September Michael Eisner became Disney's chairman and chief executive, with Frank Wells as president. Roy Disney and Stanley Gold pushed out the old management of Ron Miller after the takeover attempt in June.

headline: Britain and China agree to return Hong Kong in 1997
text: On 26 September Britain and China initialled an agreement under which Hong Kong goes back to China in 1997. Britain's lease on the New Territories, most of the colony's land, runs out that year. China promised to keep Hong Kong's economic and legal systems basically unchanged for 50 years.

headline: The prime rate falls for the first time in a year and a half
text: Banks cut the prime rate from 13% to 12.75% on 27 September, the first cut since February 1983. The rate had climbed from 11.5% in March to 13% in June, so the cut was a first sign that borrowing was getting cheaper again.

headline: Schlumberger agrees to merge with the drilling firm Sedco
text: Sedco, an offshore drilling company, agreed in September to merge with Schlumberger, the oil services group. Sedco began in 1947 as the Southeastern Drilling Company and drills wells in deep water for oil companies. The deal adds drilling rigs at sea to Schlumberger's business of measuring what lies underground.

headline: An IRA bomb in Brighton just misses Margaret Thatcher
text: The IRA bombed the Brighton hotel where British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher was staying on 12 October. Five people died and 31 were hurt.

headline: The BBC reports famine in Ethiopia
text: On 23 October the BBC reported famine in Ethiopia, with thousands dead and 10 million people at risk. The reporter Michael Buerk called it a biblical famine in the 20th century, and the film shocked viewers in Britain, who sent large donations to relief agencies.

headline: India's Prime Minister Indira Gandhi is assassinated
text: Indira Gandhi was shot dead by Sikh security guards on 31 October. Her son Rajiv Gandhi became prime minister, and riots against Sikhs followed.

headline: The prime rate falls to 12%
text: Banks cut the prime rate to 12.5% on 16 October and to 12% on 24 October. It had been 13% in June.

headline: Philip Morris's bellhop Johnny is going to the Smithsonian
text: The red uniform worn by Johnny, the tiny bellhop who shouted Call for Philip Morris, is to go on show in November at the Smithsonian's museum of American history. Albert Altieri, 4 feet 10 inches tall, was hired in 1935 and played Johnny for 25 years. He retired in 1982 after 47 years with the company, and is now 69.

headline: Reagan wins re-election in a landslide; unemployment is down to 7.2%
text: Ronald Reagan beat Walter Mondale on 6 November with 59% of the vote and 49 of the 50 states. Unemployment stands at 7.2%, down from 10.8% in December 1982.

headline: Mercedes presents the W124, successor to its W123 range
text: Daimler-Benz showed the W124, which replaces the W123 generation, to the press on 26 November in Seville, Spain. Customer deliveries are due in January 1985.

headline: Sony brings out the first portable CD player, the D-50
text: Sony released the D-50 in November, the first portable compact disc player. It cost 49,800 yen, about half the price of Sony's full-size CD player, and was one-tenth its size, about as big as four CD cases stacked up.

headline: Pop stars record 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' for Ethiopia
text: On 25 November a group of British pop stars recorded the charity single "Do They Know It's Christmas?" under the name Band Aid, in one day at a studio in London. Bob Geldof and Midge Ure wrote it, inspired by the BBC reports on the Ethiopian famine, to raise money for relief.

headline: Bankgesellschaft buys 29.9% of London's Phillips & Drew
text: In November Bankgesellschaft bought 29.9% of Phillips & Drew, a London firm that is a leading dealer in British government bonds and a big manager of investors' money. The firm has 60 partners and 593 staff.

headline: Poison gas leaks at a Union Carbide plant in Bhopal
text: On 3 December a leak of methyl isocyanate gas from a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, killed thousands of people. It is among the worst industrial disasters ever.

headline: The Dow ends 1984 down 3.7% as interest rates fall
text: The Dow Jones average closed 1984 at 1,211.57, down 3.74% after a year of strong gains in 1983. The prime rate came down to 10.75% on 19 December, from a peak of 13% in June.

headline: IBM's PC has become the standard in big offices
text: IBM sold more than 750,000 personal computers in 1983, beating its own plans by as much as 800 percent, and at one point shipped 40,000 a month. A 1983 study found that two-thirds of large companies choosing one computer picked the IBM PC and only 9% Apple. Apple keeps loyal schools and creative users.

headline: Siemens bets on memory chips
text: This year Siemens launched the MEGA project, with Philips and with government help, to develop memory chips that hold 1 and 4 million bits. US and Japanese firms lead the chip industry, and Siemens aims at world leadership in chip development within five years.

headline: Boeing's 737-300 enters service
text: USAir received the first 737-300 on 28 November, and the plane began flying passengers in December with Southwest Airlines. It seats 126 to 149 people and has CFM56 engines that burn less fuel and are quieter than older 737s, and it competes with the McDonnell Douglas MD-80.
